meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ообщить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'inform / report'.

examples.trans: By the way, I must inform you of something.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и сообщить вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and inform on time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'частье'). Common neuter noun meaning 'happiness' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: How much money is needed for happiness?

examples.text: Сколько миллионов нужно человеку для счастья?
examples.trans: How many millions does a person need for happiness?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to beat, to hit', paired with 'побить'.

examples.text: Почему меня все бьют в этом доме?
examples.trans: Why does everyone beat me in this house?

examples.text: Тише, Ваня, осторожно! Зачем ты бьёшь дерево ногой?
examples.trans: Easy, Vanya, be careful! Why are you kicking the tree with your foot?

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'health' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Конфликты с соседями угрожают здоровью подсудимого.
examples.trans: Conflicts with the neighbours threaten the defendant's health.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to drive in, hammer into'.

related.gloss: not to to drive in (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Вбей ему это счастье в счет.
examples.trans: Put all of that good luck straight onto his bill.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет вбить без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to drive in without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'account, bill, score' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Или счёт в банке. Потому что они все обманщики.
examples.trans: Or a bank account. Because they are all cheats.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'колотить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to smash, break all'.

examples.trans: He is going to smash every dish we have.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет переколотить без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to smash without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'for nothing, in vain', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Вы зря теряете время. Шпионить для вас я не буду.
examples.trans: You're wasting your time. I'm not going to spy for you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

examples.text: Мы сюда зачем прилетели? Я сразу сказал: с ним ничего не получится.
examples.trans: What did we even fly out here for? I said from the start: nothing will come of it with him.
Why did you even come here? Empty-handed!

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to come, to arrive', paired with 'приходить'.

examples.trans: Security will be here any moment.

examples.text: Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
examples.trans: Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тарик'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'old man' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This old man is sitting on the bench.
The old man told an interesting story.

examples.text: Я не могу спать спокойно! Этот старик крадёт у девушки лучшие годы.
examples.trans: I cannot sleep in peace! This old man is stealing the girl's best years.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Do you think that's really possible?
It's realistic to do that in a day.

examples.text: Я не шучу и реально сваливаю отсюда.
examples.trans: I am not joking and am seriously getting out of here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'бить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to kill, clobber (colloq.)'.

examples.text: Шеф реально тебя прибьет, если увидит.
examples.trans: The Chef will literally kill you if he sees you.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет прибить без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to kill without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'if', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'видеть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to see', paired with 'видеть'.

examples.text: И Нину свою ты больше не увидишь!
examples.trans: And you'll never see your Nina again!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from; of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

отстать.gloss: to fall behind, to leave alone

meanings.en: to fall behind, to leave alone
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'стать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to fall behind, to leave alone', paired with 'отставать'.

examples.trans: He was left behind by the train.

examples.text: Пожалуйста, немедленно отстань от нашей семьи!
examples.trans: Please, immediately leave our family alone!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'bye', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'говорить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to have a talk', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.text: Поговори с Аракеляном. Пусть он заберёт заявление.
examples.trans: Talk to Arakelyan. Get him to withdraw his statement.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'too, also', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы же здесь выросли. И о людях тоже надо думать.
examples.trans: After all, we grew up here. And you have to think about people too.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'someday, one day, ever', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Когда-нибудь ты захочешь помириться со своим папой.
examples.trans: Someday you will want to make up with your dad.

examples.text: Вы любили когда-нибудь? Смотрите, мэр стоит на коленях!
examples.trans: Have you ever loved? Look, the mayor is on his knees!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'везти'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'got lucky', paired with 'везти'.

examples.trans: A lucky break: Tretyakov called back.
Soon this chronicle will be taken back.

examples.text: Мне обязательно сегодня должно повезти здесь.
examples.trans: I definitely must get lucky here today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'already', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.
